questions.title: Explain impact of Unidirectional behaviour of React on application architecture.

content.text: - Since data flows in a single direction (from parent to child), it is easier to trace the source of any state or data change in the application.

- Components can only receive data via props and cannot directly modify their parent’s state. This strict control over data flow ensures clarity in how components interact and eliminates unintended side effects.
- The unidirectional data flow fits naturally into React's component-based architecture. Each component is responsible for rendering based on its props and state.
- Since the flow of data is always in one direction, you can pinpoint where and why a change occurs in the application.

- React’s unidirectional flow aligns well with state management libraries like Redux or Zustand. The global state can only be updated through defined actions or events, ensuring predictable state updates.
- React avoids the complexities of synchronizing data between the UI and the model which eliminates bugs related to circular updates and keeps data synchronization straightforward.

questions.title: What is virtual DOM and how does it increase performance?

content.text: in-memory representation of the actual DOM
that React uses to manage and update the UI efficiently.
When a component is first rendered, React creates a virtual DOM tree that mirrors the actual DOM structure.
of a component change, React creates a new virtual DOM tree that reflects the changes.
React compares the new virtual DOM tree with the previous one using the diffing algorithm and identifies what has changed.
This comparison identifies the minimal set of changes (or "diffs") needed to update the real DOM efficiently. - calculates updates only for the changed nodes leaving the rest nodes intact.
On completion of diffing, React applies these changes to the Real DOM. This process is called Reconciliation.
React applies all the changes in a single, efficient batch, minimizing the number of interactions with the actual DOM.
Once the diffing algorithm identifies the changes, React updates the actual DOM to reflect the new Virtual DOM. This process is optimized to be as efficient as possible.
Direct DOM manipulations are slow because the DOM is complex and browser rendering is expensive.
Virtual DOM reduces the number of direct manipulations by applying only the necessary changes.
diffing algorithm quickly identifies the differences between virtual DOM trees, ensuring only the changed elements are updated, leading to faster UI updates.
React applies all the changes in a single, efficient batch, minimizing the number of interactions with the actual DOM and reducing the multiple re-renders.
By updating the actual DOM only when necessary and in a targeted manner, React avoids unnecessary reflows and repaints, which can be costly in terms of performance.

. These fibers can be processed incrementally over multiple frames, allowing React to prioritize updates.

questions.title: What are portals in React?

content.text: React Portals are a feature in React that allows developers to render components outside of their parent component's DOM hierarchy.

Even though a portal renders outside its parent hierarchy, it still maintains the React context. It means child components can still access the context provided by their parent components, ensuring that event bubbling and state management remain intact.
Use Cases: This capability is particularly useful for creating overlays like
: Displaying modal dialogs that should overlay other content.
: Positioning tooltips that may need to escape the bounds of their parent elements.
: Ensuring dropdown menus can be rendered at the correct position without being clipped by parent containers

questions.title: What is Reactive Programming?

content.text: Reactive programming is a programming paradigm that focuses on reacting to changes and events in a
In reactive programming, components react to changes in the flow of data over time, often by using observables, observers, and event-driven architectures.
Google Search, Chat applications, financial dashboards, real-time notifications, and collaborative tools.
Different ways to implement reactive programming in React
State and props : Reacting to changes in local component state and passing data reactively through props.
React Hooks : Leveraging useState and useEffect hooks to manage state and side effects
Event Handling : Reacting to user interactions through event handling and updating state accordingly
Context API : Sharing and managing global state reactively across components using Context API

Component Lifecycle Methods : For handling side effects and updates reactively.
RxJS and observables : Leveraging RxJS for handling async operations and data streams in reactive manner.
